evidence.source: CASE 報科學, 江柏毅
evidence.text: The article reports 文 in late Shang oracle-bone and bronze inscriptions. It describes human-shaped forms resembling 大, with a prominent upper body and variable chest marks; in Western Zhou bronze forms the marks become dots or short strokes and sometimes disappear, followed by further simplification through Warring States, seal, clerical, and regular scripts. The author reports early uses chiefly as a modifier in royal names and as an honorific for rulers and ancestors. It presents the tattoo reading as a longstanding interpretation, but discusses Liu Yuan's alternative reading of 文邑 as 大邑 and 文 as meaning ‘great’; that interpretation is argued, not settled. The article also notes that proposed ca. 2000 BCE Taosi signs are too few to establish a writing system or continuity with Shang 文.
evidence.title: 甲骨和金文的「文」字真的和「文身」有關嗎？

evidence.text: The character page indexes forms under oracle-bone script, bronze inscriptions (including inscription 集成02318), Chu bamboo manuscripts, small seal, and Shuowen. The text page labels the script categories but does not itself establish what the ancient chest marks depict or mean.

evidence.source: Xu Shen, Shuowen Jiezi (quotation preserved in inspected character reference)
evidence.text: The cited Shuowen explanation is 「錯畫也。象交文。凡文之屬皆从文。」, conventionally rendered as crossed/intersecting markings and an image of interwoven pattern. This is an early Han interpretive account of the seal form; it does not independently establish the Shang graph's referent.
evidence.title: 文 - Dong Chinese dictionary

evidence.source: CASE 報科學, citing Liu Yuan (2016) and earlier studies
evidence.text: The article says the tattoo explanation has been common and describes earlier variants, including a tattooed body or crossed garment collars. It reports Liu Yuan's proposal that Shang 文 could correspond to 大, based partly on the oracle-bone phrase 文邑受禾 and parallels such as 文 / 大 in inscriptions and ancestor epithets. The article's author favors a ‘great’ interpretation, while acknowledging that this does not explain why the graph contains the chest mark. The sound/shape account and the semantic interpretation therefore remain disputed.
evidence.title: 甲骨和金文的「文」字真的和「文身」有關嗎？

evidence.text: This reference describes 文 as a pictograph of a person with writing, possibly a tattoo, on the chest, with the mark reduced to a dot or omitted in later scripts. It lists modern senses including writing, literature, and culture, and gives Baxter–Sagart-formatted Old Chinese *mə[n], Middle Chinese mjun, and Mandarin wén. These are reference summaries, not independent proof of the proposed original depiction or a dated semantic chain.

The chest marks' referent is unsettled: tattoo, other body marking, garment-related interpretations, and the 文/大 ‘great’ analysis are discussed. The evidence inspected does not establish that 文 originally meant ‘tattoo’.

The claim that 文 was the graphic original of 紋, and any proposed derivation from 煤, were not independently substantiated; neither should be asserted as established here.
